title: Every Word at Once: How the Transformer Learned to Pay Attention

source.title: Attention Is All You Need
source.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
source.venue: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017)

intro.summary: The paper asks whether a translation system can drop the slow, word-by-word reading used by earlier networks and rely only on 'attention', a way for each word to look directly at every other word. The authors built such a system, the Transformer, and tested it on two standard English-to-German and English-to-French translation benchmarks and on English sentence parsing. It scored higher than earlier systems on the BLEU score, an automatic measure of how closely a machine translation matches human translations, and it trained in a fraction of the time. The limits: tests cover text tasks only, BLEU is an imperfect automatic score, attention's cost grows with the square of sentence length, and the paper gives two different English-to-French scores (41.8 in the abstract and table, 41.0 in the results text). This lesson covers the core attention calculation, its scaling trick, position signals and the speed argument. It leaves for follow-up the parts it does not teach: multi-head attention in depth, the encoder–decoder layout, masking in the decoder, the feed-forward layers, residual connections and the training schedule.
background: A neural network is a computer program with millions of adjustable numbers that it tunes, from examples, until its outputs match the right answers.
Inside such networks, each word is stored as a list of numbers, called a vector, so that words with similar meanings get similar lists.
Before this paper, the best translation systems read a sentence one word at a time, passing a running summary from each word to the next, like a game of telephone.
Machine translation quality is often scored with BLEU, which counts how many short word sequences in the machine's output also appear in human reference translations; higher is better.
intro.aha: A network that throws away step-by-step reading entirely, letting every word look at every other word in one step, translated better than all earlier systems while training in as little as 12 hours on one machine.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: In 2017 the best translation systems read sentences one word after another. Each step had to wait for the step before it, so a computer could not spread the work across many processors at once. Long sentences made this worse, and information from early words had to survive many hand-offs to reach later ones. The authors asked whether this step-by-step reading was needed at all.
primer.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: They built the Transformer, a network that never reads word by word. Instead, every word asks a question of every other word at the same moment, scores how relevant each one is, and takes a weighted blend of what the relevant words carry. This is called attention. The network has no built-in sense of word order, so the authors added a 'position stamp' to each word. They trained it on millions of sentence pairs, using one machine with 8 graphics processors.
primer.quote: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: On English-to-German, the large Transformer beat every earlier system, including groups of systems combined together, by more than 2 BLEU points. The smaller base model also beat all earlier results, and it trained in about 12 hours. On English-to-French, it set a new best score for a single model at a fraction of earlier training costs. The paper reports this score as 41.8 in the abstract and table but 41.0 in the results text, so the exact figure is uncertain. It also did well at parsing English grammar, a task it was not designed for.
primer.quote: Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The result showed that direct word-to-word connections could replace step-by-step reading, and that this made training much faster on parallel hardware. Attention has a price, though. Every word compares itself with every other word, so the work grows with the square of sentence length, and very long inputs become expensive. The authors name this themselves and suggest restricting attention to nearby words. The evidence covers two translation benchmarks and one parsing task. BLEU is an automatic score, not a human judgment of quality.
primer.quote: To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position.

concepts.title: Scoring a match: the dot product
concepts.idea: Multiplying two lists of numbers position by position and adding up the results gives a score that is large when the lists point the same way, near zero when they are unrelated, and negative when they point opposite ways.

predict.question: Lists can be longer than two numbers. Your movie tastes are the list (2, −1, 1) for (action, romance, comedy): positive means you like it, negative means you dislike it. Each movie has a list of how much of each it contains. Which movie gives a match score of exactly zero with your tastes?
options: Movie P: (3, 0, 1)
Movie Q: (0, 3, 0)
Movie R: (1, 2, 0)
Movie S: (1, 1, 1)
why: Its numbers look different from yours, which can feel like 'unrelated'. But 2×3 + (−1)×0 + 1×1 = 7: it is heavy exactly where you are positive, so it is a strong match.
It shares none of the things you like, so it might seem neutral. But romance meets your −1: 0 + (−1)×3 + 0 = −3. That is a clash, a negative score, not zero.
Correct: 2×1 + (−1)×2 + 1×0 = 2 − 2 + 0 = 0. The action you like and the romance you dislike cancel exactly. These two lists sit at a right angle, just in three directions instead of two.
A bit of everything looks balanced. But 2×1 + (−1)×1 + 1×1 = 2, so it is a mild match. The products add up to more than zero.

terms.means: A list of numbers. With two numbers it can be drawn as an arrow from the centre.
How many numbers a list holds: 2 in this picture, 64 in the paper's main setting
Multiply two equal-length lists position by position, then add the results to get one score

model.title: Two arrows and their match score
model.note: Teaching model: the paper's lists have 64 numbers each (Section 3.2.2). Here they have only 2, so each list can be drawn as an arrow on a flat plane. Arrow A's length is fixed at 3. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Two arrows start at the centre. Each one is just two numbers: how far east its tip sits, and how far north. These boxes show them.
This slider swings arrow B around the circle.
This one turns arrow A.
And this one stretches or shrinks arrow B.
The match score turns all four numbers into a single number. Next you'll see how.

explore.prompt: Your turn. Swing and stretch the arrows and predict the match score before you look at it.

goals.text: Make the match score as negative as this model allows
hints: A negative score means the arrows disagree. What does the strongest possible disagreement look like?
Point B straight away from A and watch the angle box. Then ask what B's length does to the size of the score.
When the angle box shows its largest possible value, the score is as negative as that direction can make it. Its size still grows with B's length.

goals.text: Leave arrow B exactly where it starts, and turn only arrow A until the two arrows are unrelated: a match score of zero
hints: A score of zero means the lists are unrelated. What angle between the arrows gives that?
B points straight north, so its first number is zero. Only A's second number times B's second number is left in the sum.
A needs no north-or-south part at all. Two directions do that, and either one works.

feedback.correct: Right. The score is the sum of the position-by-position products, and here a positive product (action: 2×1) and a negative product (romance: −1×2) cancel exactly. Zero means the lists are at a right angle, even with three numbers.
feedback.incorrect: It's tempting to judge the match by eye, for example 'shares nothing I like' or 'has a bit of everything'. The score is only multiply-and-add: work out each product, keep its sign, and add them up. Zero happens when positive and negative products cancel.

steps.say: Point both arrows east. A is the list (3, 0) and so is B. A list of numbers like this is called a vector. How many numbers it holds is its dimension, which is 2 here.
Now score them. Multiply the first numbers: 3 × 3 = 9. Multiply the second numbers: 0 × 0 = 0. Add them: 9. This multiply-then-add recipe is called the dot product.
Turn B by 45°. Its numbers become about (2.1, 2.1). Now 3 × 2.1 + 0 × 2.1 ≈ 6.4. The arrows are less alike, so the score is smaller.
At a right angle, B is (0, 3). 3 × 0 + 0 × 3 = 0. Wherever one list has something, the other has nothing. A score of zero means unrelated.
Keep turning. B now leans west, so its first number is negative: 3 × (−2.1) + 0 × 2.1 ≈ −6.4. When the arrows point apart, the score goes negative.
Fully opposite: 3 × (−3) = −9. That is the lowest score this pair of lengths can reach.
Length matters too. Point B east again but shrink it to 1, and the score is only 3. Direction decides the sign. Length scales the size.
Last, turn both arrows to 60° and lengthen B. Every number changed: A ≈ (1.5, 2.6), B ≈ (2, 3.5). Yet 1.5 × 2 + 2.6 × 3.5 ≈ 12, the top score here. Only how the arrows line up matters.

understand.explanation: Multiply two lists of numbers position by position and add the results, and you get one score for how well they line up: the dot product. Lists pointing the same way give a large positive score. Lists at a right angle give zero. Opposite lists give a negative score, and longer lists make the score bigger in size. The Transformer uses exactly this score to judge how well two words' lists match. In its main setting each list has 64 numbers (Section 3.2.2), not the 2 drawn here. The paper prefers it over a rival scoring method that uses a small neural network mainly because it is pure multiplying and adding, which computers do very fast in bulk. The authors also note a limit: making the lists shorter hurt translation quality, which they read as a hint that a more sophisticated matching score than the dot product might help (Section 6.2).
understand.quote: While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

equation.text: q · k = Σ_{i=1}^{d_{k}} q_{i}k_{i}   →   with two numbers:

connect.caption: The left side is the paper's own formula (footnote 4, Section 3.2.1). The paper calls the two lists q and k, names you will meet soon. Σ means 'add up', and d_{k} is how many numbers each list holds: 64 in the paper, 2 in this model. On the right, a_{1} and a_{2} (blue) are arrow A's first and second numbers, b_{1} and b_{2} (orange) are arrow B's, and their multiply-and-add gives the match score.

concepts.recap: Multiply two lists position by position and add: same direction gives a big positive score, a right angle gives zero, opposite directions give a negative score.

activities.prompt: Same two arrow lengths, three different angles between them. Compare the match score in each.
activities.takeaway: Only the angle changed, and the score went from +9 through 0 to −9. The sign of the dot product says whether the lists agree, are unrelated, or disagree.

concepts.title: Turning scores into shares: softmax
concepts.idea: Softmax turns any set of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, giving the highest score the largest share and exaggerating gaps between scores.

predict.question: Start from cat = 2, mat = 1, left = 0. Now add 10 to every score, so they become 12, 11 and 10. What happens to the three shares?
options: They stay exactly the same
Cat's share grows, because bigger scores get exaggerated more
The shares even out, because a +10 swamps the small differences
The shares add up to more than 100%
why: Right: shares depend only on the gaps between scores. Adding 10 to everyone multiplies every word's e^score by the same factor (e¹⁰), and that factor cancels when each is divided by the total.
It is tempting to think large scores are favoured. What softmax exaggerates is the gaps, and the gaps (1 and 1) have not changed, so cat keeps the same share.
This would hold if shares were scores divided by their sum, because 12 : 11 : 10 is nearly even. Softmax works on the gaps, and those are unchanged, so the split stays about 67 / 24 / 9.
Dividing by the total always makes the shares add to exactly 100%, however large the scores are.

terms.means: The rule that turns a list of scores into positive shares that add up to 1 (100%): raise e to each score, then divide each result by their total
Raising the number e ≈ 2.718 to a power (written e^x). It is always positive, and each extra point multiplies the result by about 2.7

model.title: Three match scores become three shares of attention
model.note: Teaching model: one word ('it' in 'The cat left the mat because it was tired') has hand-set match scores for just three other words. In the Transformer these scores come from learned dot products, and softmax may run over many more entries. The rule that turns scores into shares is exact, but the scores are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Take the sentence 'The cat left the mat because it was tired.' The word 'it' looks back and gives three words a match score, just like the scores from the last lesson.
Each slider is one word's match score. Higher means a better match. A score can be any number, even below zero.
Each coloured bar is the share of 'it's attention that the word gets, out of 100%.
The grey bar adds the three shares together.
Watch: give 'mat' a higher score and see how the bars move.

explore.prompt: Now steer the shares yourself. The bars respond only to the three scores, so think about the gaps between scores rather than the scores alone.

goals.text: Make all three words get an equal share of the attention
hints: When would two words end up with the same share?
Shares depend on the gaps between scores, not on how big the scores are.
You need no gap at all between any two words. Any common score will do, and one word already has a score you could match.

goals.text: Split the attention evenly between cat and mat, while 'left' gets less than 5%
hints: There are two jobs: make cat and mat tie, then make 'left' nearly vanish.
Cat and mat tie only when their scores are equal. Then lower 'left' until it sits far enough below the pair.
A gap of 2 between 'left' and the tied pair still leaves 'left' a little over 5%. Open the gap a bit further.

feedback.correct: Yes. Softmax only cares about gaps. Adding the same amount to every score multiplies every e^score by the same factor. That factor cancels when each is divided by the total, so the shares stay about 67%, 24% and 9%.
feedback.incorrect: You may have pictured shares as scores divided by their sum, or as favouring big numbers in themselves. Softmax raises e to each score and then divides by the total, so only the differences between scores matter. Shifting every score by 10 leaves the gaps unchanged, so the shares stay the same.

steps.say: Start here: cat scores 2, mat 1, left 0. The shares come out at about 67%, 24% and 9%.
However you set the scores, the total is always 100%. The rule that turns scores into shares like this is called softmax.
Push 'left' well below zero. Its share shrinks towards 0 but never goes negative, and the share it loses goes to the other two.

How does it work? Softmax raises e, about 2.718, to the power of each score. This is called the exponential, and it is always positive. Then softmax divides each result by their total, so the shares add up to 1.
Compare cat and mat. Their scores differ by only 1, yet cat gets about 2.7 times mat's share.
Widen the gap to 3 by lowering mat. Now cat gets about 20 times as much. Each extra point of gap multiplies the advantage by 2.7, so softmax exaggerates gaps.
Finally, let mat jump past cat. The top score always takes the biggest share. Mat now gets about 88%, and cat falls to about 12%, even though cat's own score never moved.

understand.explanation: Softmax takes a list of scores, which can be any numbers, and turns them into shares that are always positive and always add up to 100%. It raises e to each score (the exponential) and divides each result by the total. Because of the exponential, each extra point of gap multiplies the leader's advantage by about 2.7, so modest gaps in score become large gaps in share. Raising one word's score therefore takes share away from all the others, and only the gaps between scores matter. The paper does not test softmax itself. It uses this standard rule as a building block: to turn the decoder's final output into probabilities for the next word and, as the next lesson shows, to turn match scores into attention weights.
understand.quote: softmax function to convert the decoder output to predicted next-token probabilities.

connect.caption: This is the standard softmax rule the model uses. The paper relies on it but does not write it out. Each coloured s is the match score from the slider of the same colour (cat, mat, left), and exp(s) is the exponential: e raised to that score. The left side is the cat bar. Put mat's or left's exp on top instead to get their shares. All three shares divide by the same total, so they always add to 1.

concepts.recap: Softmax turns any scores into positive shares that add to 100%, and every extra point of gap multiplies the leader's advantage by about 2.7.

activities.question: Imagine just two words, one scoring exactly 2 points higher than the other. What share (in %) does the higher-scoring word get?
activities.explanation: A gap of 2 means the leader's exponential is e² ≈ 7.4 times the other's. The split is 7.4 parts to 1 part, and 7.4 ÷ 8.4 ≈ 88%. A gap of just 2 points already gives nearly a 9-to-1 split.
hints: Only the gap matters, so give the lower word e⁰ = 1 part.
The leader then gets e² parts, which is about 2.7 × 2.7.

concepts.title: Attention: ask, score, blend
concepts.idea: A word's query is scored against every word's key, softmax turns the scores into weights, and the word's new meaning is the weighted blend of all the words' values.

predict.question: A fifth word, 'dog', is added to the sentence. It has exactly the same label and hands over exactly the same meaning as 'animal'. 'it' still looks strongly for a living thing. What happens?
options: Both 'animal' and 'dog' keep the share 'animal' had alone, so the shares add up to more than 100%
'animal' loses share to 'dog', but the blend still means a living thing, even slightly more so
'dog' gets almost nothing, because 'animal' already matched the question
The blend becomes twice as much 'living thing' as before
why: Tempting if each match feels independent. But softmax shares always add up to 100%, so two equal matches must split the share between them.

Correct. 'animal' and 'dog' get equal scores, so they split the top share. Together they take even more than 'animal' did alone. Both hand over the same living-thing meaning, so the blend still means a living thing.
Tempting if attention seems to pick one winner. Softmax gives every word a share based only on its own score. Equal scores get equal shares, so 'dog' gets as much as 'animal'.
Tempting if blending seems to add meanings up. The blend is a weighted average with shares that sum to 1. It can never go past the meaning of the most 'living thing' word, which is 100% here.

terms.means: What a word is looking for, written as a short list of numbers
A word's label: the list of numbers that every query is scored against
What a word hands over to the blend, kept separate from its label
Every word in a sentence doing ask, score and blend at the same time, over the same sentence

model.title: How much 'it' looks at each word, and what 'it' ends up meaning
model.note: Teaching model: the made-up sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired'. Only four of its words are shown, with one viewpoint, from the word 'it'. Each word gets just two hand-picked numbers (living thing, place) for its label and for what it hands over. The paper uses 64 learned numbers per head and 8 heads. As in the paper, each score is divided by the square root of the list length, here √2, before softmax; the next concept explains why. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Our sentence: 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired.' The first four bars show how much the word 'it' looks at each of four other words.
Those four shares always add up to 100%.
This slider sets how strongly 'it' looks for a living thing. Watch the 'animal' bar.
This one sets how strongly 'it' looks for a place. Now 'street' grows too.
The last two bars show what 'it' ends up meaning: a mix of living thing and place.

explore.prompt: You steer what 'it' is looking for. Use the ask, score and blend steps to decide what 'it' ends up meaning.

goals.text: Make 'it' clearly mean a living thing: get the blend's living-thing meaning above 90%.
hints: Even when 'it' looks hard for a living thing, some words still take shares away from 'animal'. Which ones?
'street' and 'cross' match the place part of the question. What if 'it' stops looking for a place, or looks away from places?
Push the living-thing slider near its top, then bring the place slider to zero or below while you watch the living-thing blend bar.

goals.text: Make 'it' truly torn between the two candidates: give 'animal' and 'street' each more than 40% of the shares.
hints: To be torn, 'animal' and 'street' need equal scores.
Equal is not enough. At the start they are equal, but 'cross' and 'tired' still take a lot. The two top scores must also stand far above the others.
Raise both sliders together, keeping them equal, until both bars pass 40%.

feedback.correct: Right. Shares come from softmax, so they always add up to 1. Two words with equal scores split the top share between them. The blend is a weighted average, so it still means a living thing because both words hand over that meaning.
feedback.incorrect: The likely assumption is that each word's share is set on its own, or that blending adds meanings up. In fact softmax makes every share depend on all the scores, and the total is always 100%. The blend is a weighted average, so it can never be more 'living thing' than the most living-thing word.

steps.say: First, 'it' looks for nothing at all. Every match score is 0, so softmax splits the shares evenly: 25% each. What a word is looking for, as a list of numbers, is called its query.

Every word also carries a label, called its key. 'animal' has the key (2, 0): strongly 'living thing', not 'place'. Now the query looks for a living thing. Its dot product with 'animal''s key jumps, and softmax gives 'animal' about 70%.
'tired' rose a little too. Its key (1, 0) also hints at a living thing, so it gets a medium score.
Now look at 'street'. Its score did not change: it is still 0. Yet its share fell from 25% to about 4%. Shares must add up to 100%, so a strong match takes share from every other word.

The third step is the blend. Each word also hands over something, its value, kept separate from its key. 'it' takes about 70% of 'animal''s value, 17% of 'tired''s, and so on. The blend now means about 81% living thing.
Flip the question: look for a place and away from living things. 'street''s key now matches best, and the blend turns into about 95% place. The values did not change. Only the shares did.
In 'because it was tired', 'it' should mean the animal. Look for a living thing and steer away from places. 'animal' takes most of the share, and 'it' now means mostly a living thing.

In a real Transformer, every word does this at once, each with its own query, over the same sentence. This is called self-attention. The numbers in the queries, keys and values are learned in training, not set by hand.

understand.explanation: Attention works in three moves. First, a word asks a question: its query. Second, the query is scored against every word's key with a dot product, and softmax turns the scores into shares that add up to 1; a strong match takes share from every other word, even words whose scores did not move. Third, the word's new meaning is the blend of all the words' values, each counted by its share. The paper does exactly this (Section 3.2.1), with queries, keys and values learned from each word's numbers rather than hand-picked, and in self-attention all three come from the same sentence. The paper's Figure 4 shows real heads that 'apparently' link the word 'its' back to what it refers to; this is an example the authors picked, not proof of what every head does.
understand.quote: The input consists of queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv. We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

connect.caption: This is the paper's Equation 1. Q holds the queries: the two sliders are the query of 'it'. Kᵀ holds the keys: the fixed labels of 'animal', 'street', 'cross' and 'tired'. QKᵀ is every dot-product score at once. Dividing by √d_k (here √2) comes next lesson. softmax(…) gives the shares, shown as the four word bars. Multiplying by V, the values, blends what each word hands over; the result is the two blend bars.

concepts.recap: Each word asks with its query, scores every word's key, turns the scores into shares with softmax, and becomes the share-weighted blend of the words' values.

activities.title: Ask, score, blend by hand

steps.text: Ask: 'it' looks strongly for a living thing and not at all for a place, so its query is (2, 0). The keys are: animal (2, 0), street (0, 2), cross (0.5, 0.5), tired (1, 0).
Score: take the dot product of the query with each key, then divide by √2, as the paper divides by the square root of the list length.
Softmax: raise e to each score, then divide each by the total.
Blend: each word hands over its value: animal (1, 0), street (0, 1), cross (0.2, 0.4), tired (0.5, 0). Multiply each value by its share and add them up.
Read the result: 'it' now carries mostly living-thing meaning. Set the living-thing slider to 2 and the place slider to 0, and the bars show the same numbers.

activities.takeaway: Keys decide how big each share is. Values decide what each share brings. The output is just a weighted average.

activities.prompt: Think of a filing cabinet. Match each part of attention to its everyday role.

pairs.target: The search request you type in
pairs.feedback: The query is what the word is looking for. It is compared with every folder.

pairs.target: The label on each folder's tab
pairs.feedback: The key is only used for matching. It decides how well a folder fits the request.
The value is what actually gets handed over, once the label has decided how much to take.

pairs.target: How much of each folder you copy into your notes
pairs.feedback: The shares add up to 100%, so copying more from one folder means copying less from the others.

pairs.target: Your page of notes: a mix of every folder, mostly the best matches
pairs.feedback: The output is the share-weighted mix of all the values. It becomes the word's new meaning.

activities.takeaway: The label decides how much you take; the contents are what you take. That is why keys and values are kept separate.

concepts.title: Why divide by √d: keeping softmax from freezing
concepts.idea: Dot products of longer number lists tend to grow larger, which pushes softmax to put almost all weight on one word and stops the network from learning, so the paper divides every score by the square root of the list length.

predict.question: Suppose a designer wants to be extra safe and divides every score by the list length d_k itself, not by its square root. With very long lists, what would softmax do?
options: Keep the shares steady, just like dividing by √d_k
Drift toward an even split, so the best match gets lost among the others
Freeze on the top word even faster
Nothing changes, because dividing never changes which word ranks first
why: Dividing by more can look like more of the same fix. But d_k grows faster than √d_k, so the scores now shrink as lists get longer. They are not steady.
Right. The typical score size becomes √d_k ÷ d_k = 1/√d_k, which shrinks toward zero. The best match's lead shrinks with it, and softmax gives every word nearly the same share.
Freezing comes from scores that are too large. Dividing by d_k makes them smaller, so it pushes the other way.
It is true that the same word still ranks first. But softmax depends on the size of the gaps, not only their order, so the shares do change.

terms.means: The length of each query and key list. In the paper's base model it is 64 for each attention head.
The slope that tells training which way, and how far, to nudge each number. Near zero means learning stalls.
A softmax pushed so far that one word takes almost all the weight, so small changes to the scores do almost nothing.
The paper's attention: each dot-product score is divided by √d_k before softmax.

model.title: How longer lists change the best match's share and the learning signal
model.note: Teaching model: one word compares itself with ten words. The best match leads the other nine, which are tied, by a set number of 'typical score sizes'. The typical size of a raw dot product grows as the square root of the list length. This follows the paper's footnote 4, which assumes random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1. The 'learning signal' is the slope of the top word's share with respect to its own score, rescaled so that 100% is the largest possible. Real attention uses learned, non-random numbers and many more words. All numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How much the best match stands out

steps.say: One word is looking for its best match among ten. This solid curve shows how much of the weight the best match gets, for lists of different lengths.
The other solid curve is the learning signal: how strongly the network can still adjust that weight. High is healthy. Near zero means stuck.
This slider sets how many numbers are in each word's list. The vertical line marks where you are.
This slider sets how far the best match stands out from the other nine words.
This switch divides every score before softmax. The dashed curves show what happens when it is on.

explore.prompt: Make softmax freeze, then rescue it. Watch the dots ride along the solid curves with raw scores and along the dashed curves with divided scores.

goals.text: With raw scores, freeze softmax so the learning signal is under 10%, while the best match leads by less than a third of a typical score size.
hints: A weak lead can still become a big gap. What makes every raw score bigger?
Turn the stand-out slider down to a weak lead, keep the switch off, and watch the solid signal curve as the list grows.
With a lead that weak, the solid signal only falls under 10% near the far right of the length slider. With an even weaker lead it never gets there.

goals.text: Choose a list long enough that raw scores would freeze softmax ('Signal if not divided' under 10%), then rescue learning so the signal in use is back above 40%.
hints: First create the problem, then apply the paper's fix.
Grow the list until the 'Signal if not divided' box is tiny, then think about what the switch does to the typical size of a score.
Once the raw signal has collapsed, you don't need to touch the stand-out slider. One flip is enough.

feedback.correct: Dividing by d_k overshoots. The typical score size becomes 1/√d_k, which shrinks as lists grow, so the gaps vanish and softmax spreads the weight almost evenly. √d_k is exactly the amount that cancels the growth.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think that more dividing means more safety. But the aim is to keep scores at a steady size. Dividing by d_k shrinks them toward zero for long lists, and softmax of near-equal scores gives near-equal shares, so attention can no longer pick out the best match.

steps.say: Start with short lists of 4 numbers and raw scores. A score adds up 4 products, so its typical size is about 2, the square root of 4.
Now use 64 numbers. Each product pushes the sum a little one way or the other, so the typical size grows to 8, the square root of 64. The best match's lead grows with it, from 1 to 4.
Softmax exaggerates gaps. The bigger lead hands the top word about 86% of the weight, and the learning signal has fallen to about half.

At 400 numbers the top word takes essentially all the weight and the signal is near zero. That signal is the gradient, the slope training follows. When it vanishes we have a saturated softmax: frozen on one word.
The paper calls this list length d_k, the length of each query and key. In the base model each attention head uses 64.
Now switch on the fix: divide every score by √d_k. The typical size drops back to 1, so the top word keeps about 15% and the signal sits near 52%. This is scaled dot-product attention.
Slide all the way to 512. The dashed curves stay flat while the solid ones have collapsed. Dividing by √d_k cancels the growth exactly, so list length no longer freezes softmax.

understand.explanation: A dot product adds one product per number in the list, so longer lists give scores that spread out more. The paper's footnote shows that for random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1, the variance equals d_k, so the typical size grows like √d_k. Softmax exaggerates gaps, so large scores create a saturated softmax: nearly all the weight goes to one word, the gradient is almost zero, and training can barely adjust it. Dividing every score by √d_k cancels that growth and keeps scores the same typical size at any length. The paper's support is this argument plus earlier work [3] finding that dot-product attention without scaling fell behind additive attention at larger d_k. The authors say they 'suspect' this cause and do not report a run with scaling switched off, and real scores are learned rather than random, so the footnote illustrates a tendency rather than proving it.
understand.quote: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3]. We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

check.task: Show that dividing can matter even for short lists. With lists of at most 64 numbers, find a setting where raw scores would freeze softmax ('Signal if not divided' under 10%) but dividing keeps the learning signal above 40%.
check.hint: Raw softmax freezes when the top score's lead gets big. A long list is one way to make it big. What is the other?
check.misconception: That freezing depends on list length alone, so dividing by √d_k only matters for very long lists. In fact the raw lead is the stand-out amount times √d_k, so a strongly standing-out match can freeze softmax even at modest lengths.

connect.caption: This is the paper's Equation 1. QKᵀ holds every query-key dot product, the raw scores. √d_k (coloured like the list-length slider) is what the model divides by when the switch is on. Softmax turns the divided scores into the shares tracked by the top word's curve. V holds the values that get blended, as in the attention concept.

concepts.recap: Longer lists make dot products bigger by about √d_k; dividing every score by √d_k keeps softmax from freezing on one word, so the network can keep learning.

concepts.title: Stamping each word with its place
concepts.idea: Attention alone cannot tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog', so the Transformer adds to each word a pattern of sine waves of different speeds that is unique to that word's position.

predict.question: Each word now gets its position stamp added before attention runs. In 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog', the word 'bites' sits at position 1 both times. Does 'bites' still end up with the same blend in both sentences?
options: No: 'dog' at the start carries a different stamp from 'dog' at the end, so its scores and the blend change
Yes: the words are the same, so the blend is the same
No, but only because 'bites' itself has moved
Yes, because the stamp is added after attention has finished
why: Right. 'dog' at position 0 and 'dog' at position 2 now carry different number lists. Their keys and values change, so the scores, the weights and the blend all change.
That was true before the stamps. Once position numbers are added, a word's numbers depend on both what it is and where it sits.
'bites' is at position 1 in both sentences, so its own stamp is identical. The difference comes from the words around it, which have swapped places.
The paper adds the stamps at the very bottom of the network, to the input embeddings, so every attention layer sees them.

terms.means: A list of numbers, one per slot in a word's meaning list, added to that word to record where it sits in the sentence
How many positions a wave takes to go through one full rise and fall before repeating
A smooth, repeating up-and-down wave shaped like the sine function

model.title: Three waves read at two word positions
model.note: Teaching model: it uses the paper's sine formula for a tiny model whose word lists have 16 numbers, and shows only 3 of those 16 numbers (the sine rows for i = 0, 1, 2). The matching cosine rows are hidden. The paper's base model uses 512 numbers, with wavelengths running from 2π to 10000·2π positions. 'Stamp difference' is the straight-line distance over the three shown waves only. Wave heights come from the formula. Nothing here is the paper's data.

outputs.label: Stamp difference (A vs B)
outputs.expr: sqrt(pow(sin(pos) - sin(pos2), 2) + pow(sin(pos / pow(10000, 2 / 16)) - sin(pos2 / pow(10000, 2 / 16)), 2) + pow(sin(pos / pow(10000, 4 / 16)) - sin(pos2 / pow(10000, 4 / 16)), 2))

steps.say: Along the bottom are word positions in a sentence: 0 for the first word, 1 for the next, and so on up to 50.
Three waves rise and fall across those positions: a fast one, a medium one and a slow one.
This slider moves word A. The dots show the height of each wave where A sits.
This second slider places word B, so you can compare two positions side by side.
This box adds up how different A's three heights are from B's.

explore.prompt: Hunt for a pair of positions that would fool the fast wave alone, but that the full set of waves still tells apart.

goals.text: Find two different positions where the fast wave reads almost the same height (within 0.2 of each other), yet the stamp difference is above 0.8.
hints: The fast wave keeps returning to the same heights. Where else along the row does it match word A?
Put A and B a whole number of fast-wave cycles apart (each cycle is a little over six positions), then look at the slow wave's dots.
A few cycles apart, the slow wave has hardly moved. Go many cycles apart, so the slow wave has swung far from where it was at A.

feedback.correct: Yes. Once stamps are added, a word's numbers depend on where it sits as well as what it is. Swapping 'dog' and 'man' changes their keys and values, so the blend for 'bites' changes too.
feedback.incorrect: You may have pictured attention still seeing only the words. The stamps go into every word's numbers at the very start. 'dog' at position 0 and 'dog' at position 2 are now different lists, and that changes the scores and the blend for 'bites'.

steps.say: Without help, attention saw 'dog' the same way wherever it sat. The fix starts here: read every wave's height at a word's position. Word A is at position 0, where all three waves sit at 0.
Word B is at position 1. The fast wave has already climbed to 0.84, the medium to 0.31 and the slow only to 0.10. That list of heights is position 1's stamp.

The Transformer adds a stamp like this to each word's embedding, its list of meaning numbers, before any attention happens. The paper calls it a positional encoding. Now 'dog' first and 'dog' last carry different numbers.
Look at neighbours 6 and 7. The slow wave barely moves, from 0.56 to 0.64. The fast wave swings from −0.28 to 0.66. Fast waves are what separate next-door words.

But a fast wave repeats. Its wavelength, the distance for one full rise and fall, is 2π, about 6.3 positions. Positions 3 and 22 are three cycles apart, so the fast wave reads almost the same at both: 0.14 and −0.01.

The slower waves have longer wavelengths, so they have not come back around yet. The slow wave reads 0.30 at position 3 and 0.81 at position 22. Each wave is a sinusoid, and waves of different speeds rarely all line up at once.

It works like a clock. The second hand alone repeats every minute, but second, minute and hour hands together pin down the time. In the paper's model, 512 waves stretch from a wavelength of 2π up to 10000·2π positions.

understand.explanation: Attention scores words by what they contain, so on its own it treats a sentence like a bag of words: 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' give 'bites' the same blend. The Transformer fixes this by adding a positional encoding to each word's embedding at the very start, before any attention. Each number in the encoding is the height of a wave at that position. Waves of many speeds, from fast to very slow, together give every position its own pattern. The authors also tried learned position numbers instead and got nearly identical results (Table 3, row E: 25.7 against 25.8 BLEU on a development set). They kept the waves because these may let the model handle sentences longer than any seen in training, a hope the paper states but does not test.
understand.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks.

connect.caption: pos is the word's position (the Word A slider). i picks the wave: in this 16-number teaching model, i = 0 gives the fast wave, i = 1 the medium wave and i = 2 the slow wave. Each step up in i stretches the wavelength. The paper pairs each sine row with a cosine row, PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{model}}), hidden here, and uses d_{model} = 512 in the base model.

concepts.recap: Attention is blind to word order, so the Transformer adds to each word the heights of many waves of different speeds at its position, a stamp that differs from one position to the next.

activities.prompt: Attention with no position information: watch what 'bites' gets in two sentences with the same words in a different order. The scores are made up for illustration.

cases.label: dog bites man
cases.text: 'bites' asks its query. The keys score dog 2.0, bites 1.0, man 0.5. Softmax turns these into weights of about 0.63, 0.23 and 0.14. The new meaning of 'bites' = 0.63 × dog's value + 0.23 × bites' value + 0.14 × man's value.

cases.label: man bites dog
cases.text: The scores depend only on what each word is, not where it is: man 0.5, bites 1.0, dog 2.0. The weights are the same, 0.14, 0.23 and 0.63, just listed in a different order. Adding up gives exactly the same blend for 'bites'.

activities.takeaway: On its own, attention cannot tell who bit whom. Something must tell each word where it sits.

concepts.title: One step instead of a chain
concepts.idea: A recurrent network needs one back-to-back step per word, so its work can't be split up and distant words are many hand-offs apart; self-attention links every pair of words in one step but must compare every word with every other.

predict.question: A team wants to run full self-attention over a whole book of about 100,000 word pieces, with 512 numbers per word. Using this lesson's reasoning, what is the main problem they will hit?
options: The total work explodes, because every word must be compared with every other word
The layer needs about 100,000 steps in a row, one per word
The first and last words of the book end up thousands of hand-offs apart
There is no problem: one step means attention is always the cheaper choice
why: Right. Attention's work grows like n²·d. With n far above 512, it costs about 200 times a recurrent layer's work. The paper suggests limiting attention to nearby words for very long inputs.
That is the recurrent layer's problem. Attention still takes one step at any length, given enough processors to do the comparisons side by side.
That is also the recurrent layer's problem. In full self-attention any word reaches any other in one hand-off, even in a book.
One step in a row is not the same as little work. Attention's total work passes the recurrent layer's once the sentence is longer than the numbers per word.

terms.means: Steps that must happen one after another, because each one needs the result of the step before
Splitting a job into pieces that many processors can do at the same time
How many hand-offs information makes to travel from one word to another inside the network
How many numbers the network uses to describe each word, written d; 512 in the paper's base model

model.title: Steps in a row and total work as a sentence gets longer
model.note: Teaching model: it uses the per-layer counts from the paper's Table 1 with every fixed multiplier set to 1. A recurrent layer takes n steps in a row and about n·d·d multiplications. A self-attention layer takes 1 step and about n·n·d multiplications. It shows one layer only, ignoring the feed-forward part, the other layers and the limits of real hardware. 'One step' assumes enough processors to do every comparison at once. Lengths count word pieces, and work is in millions of multiplications. The numbers are illustrative, not the paper's measurements, though 512 numbers per word is the paper's base model size.

controls.label: Show total work instead of steps

outputs.label: Recurrent: hand-offs from first word to last

y.label: Steps in a row, or total work in millions (use the switch)

steps.say: Each line shows how much one layer of a network has to do. Further right means a longer sentence.
This line is a recurrent layer, which reads one word at a time. Its height counts the steps that must happen one after another.
This line is an attention layer, from the last few concepts. Notice how it hugs the floor.
This slider sets the sentence length. The marker and the two dots follow your sentence.
This slider sets how many numbers describe each word. The switch changes the picture from steps to total work.

explore.prompt: Steps in a row and total work are two different bills. Move the sentence length and the numbers per word, flip the switch, and see when each layer is the cheaper one.

goals.text: Find a sentence where the recurrent layer needs at least 100 times as many steps in a row as attention, yet attention still does less total work.
hints: Steps and total work are different bills. Watch both pairs of numbers.
Lengthen the sentence until the recurrent step count reaches 100. Then check that the work ratio is still below 1.
Attention's work stays smaller as long as the sentence is shorter than the number of numbers per word.

goals.text: Make attention do more total work than the recurrent layer while keeping the sentence shorter than the paper's 512 numbers per word.
hints: With 512 numbers per word, attention is cheaper for any sentence shorter than 512. Which other slider moves the point where the work curves cross?
Flip to total work. The curves cross where the sentence length equals the numbers per word.
Pick a sentence of a few hundred words. Then lower the numbers per word until they drop below the sentence length.

feedback.correct: Yes. Attention's work grows like n²·d, so for a book-length input with n far above d it becomes much more expensive than a recurrent layer. Its single step and single hand-off don't change that.
feedback.incorrect: It's easy to carry over the recurrent layer's weak spots, or to think one step means little work. Attention keeps one step and one hand-off at any length. What grows is the number of word-pair comparisons, and that makes very long inputs expensive.

steps.say: Start with a 10-word sentence. A recurrent network reads word 1 and passes a summary on to word 2, then word 3, and so on. That makes 10 steps, each waiting for the one before.
Lengthen it to 100 words: now there are 100 steps in a row. Steps like these are called sequential operations. No step can start until the previous one ends.
Splitting a job across many processors is called parallelization. Here it is blocked, so extra processors cannot shorten the chain. Long sentences simply take longer.
Attention scores each word against every word, and none of those scores waits for another. They can all run side by side, so the layer takes 1 step at any sentence length.

Distance matters too. In a 500-word sentence, news from word 1 is handed along 499 times before it reaches the last word. The number of hand-offs is the path length. In attention it is 1, because any word reads any other directly.

Now flip to total work. The numbers per word are the representation dimension, written d. A recurrent layer does about d×d multiplications per word, so n·d² in all. Attention compares n×n pairs of words at d multiplications each, so n²·d.
At 40 words with d = 512, attention does less than a tenth of the recurrent layer's work.

Stretch the sentence to 800 words. Attention's curve bends upward and passes the recurrent line at 512 words, where the length equals d. That is the trade: one step and one hand-off, paid for by comparing every word with every other.

understand.explanation: A recurrent layer handles words one after another. A sentence of n words therefore needs n steps in a row, and that work cannot be split across processors. News from the first word also reaches the last only after n−1 hand-offs. Self-attention compares every pair of words at once, so it needs one step, and every pair of words is one hand-off apart. The price is that the comparisons grow with n², so its total work (n²·d) beats a recurrent layer's (n·d²) only while sentences are shorter than the representation dimension d. The paper makes this argument in Section 4 and Table 1 by counting operations, not by timing them. It notes that translation sentences split into word pieces are usually shorter than d. For the claim that shorter paths make long-range links easier to learn, it relies on earlier work, and for very long inputs it suggests restricting attention to nearby words as future work.
understand.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

check.task: Put the model in a state where attention and the recurrent layer do almost the same total work, using fewer than 512 numbers per word.
check.hint: The total-work curves cross at one special sentence length. How does that length relate to the numbers per word?
check.misconception: That attention's single step means it always does less total work, or that the break-even sentence length is fixed. In fact the work is equal where the sentence length equals d, so the break-even point moves whenever d changes.

connect.caption: These are the paper's Table 1 rows for a recurrent layer and a self-attention layer. O(…) means 'grows like', ignoring fixed multipliers; the model sets those multipliers to 1. n is the sentence-length slider and d is the numbers-per-word slider. The step counts match the two step boxes. Table 1 also lists the longest path as O(n) for recurrent layers and O(1) for self-attention, the hand-offs you watched. Dividing the two work terms gives n/d, so the curves cross where n = d.

concepts.recap: Attention swaps a chain of n steps for one step and one hand-off, but its work grows with n², so it is cheaper only while sentences are shorter than d.

concepts.title: Better and faster: weighing the evidence
concepts.idea: On standard translation benchmarks the Transformer beat earlier systems on BLEU at a fraction of their training cost, and removing or changing its parts shows which ones matter, within the limits of an automatic score and a few tasks.

terms.means: A fixed, public test set that every team scores its system on in the same way, so results can be compared fairly
Several separately trained networks whose answers are combined; usually more accurate, but costs several times as much to train
Floating-point operations: a count of the arithmetic steps a computer does, used here as a measure of training cost
Changing or removing one part of a system, retraining it and seeing how much the score drops, to learn which parts matter

concepts.recap: Using only attention, the Transformer set translation records at far lower training cost; ablations show which parts matter, within the limits of BLEU and two news tasks.

understand.explanation: To test the Transformer, the authors used a benchmark: a fixed, public test set, here WMT 2014 news sentences in English-to-German and English-to-French. Every system on a benchmark is graded the same way, with BLEU, the automatic score of how much a translation's wording overlaps with human translations. The Transformer was compared with earlier single networks and with an ensemble or two. An ensemble is a team of several trained networks whose answers are combined; it usually scores higher but costs more to train. The authors also estimated each system's training cost in FLOPs, a count of the arithmetic operations the computers performed, from training time, number of GPUs and each GPU's speed. Each ablation changed one part of the model, retrained it and watched the score, to show which parts matter. Limits: BLEU measures word overlap, not human judgment; the tests cover two language pairs of news text plus one grammar task; and each variant was trained once, with no error bars.
understand.quote: On the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, the big transformer model (Transformer (big) in Table 2) outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0 BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4.

activities.prompt: English-to-German news test, from the paper's Table 2. Read the BLEU score (higher is better) and the estimated training cost (lower is cheaper) together.

cases.label: Best earlier entry: ConvS2S ensemble
cases.text: 26.36 BLEU. Training cost about 7.7 × 10^19 FLOPs. This team of several convolutional networks was the strongest result before the Transformer.

cases.label: Transformer (base)
cases.text: 27.3 BLEU, already above every earlier entry, ensembles included. Training cost about 3.3 × 10^18 FLOPs, roughly 23 times less than that ensemble. Trained for 12 hours on one machine with 8 GPUs.

cases.label: Transformer (big)
cases.text: 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 points above every earlier entry. Training cost about 2.3 × 10^19 FLOPs, still under a third of the ConvS2S ensemble. Trained for 3.5 days on the same machine.

activities.takeaway: Usually a better score costs more computing. Here the score went up and the cost went down. Two cautions. First, the costs are the authors' estimates from training time and GPU speed, not direct measurements. Second, for English-to-French the abstract and Table 2 give the big model 41.8 BLEU, but the text of Section 6.1 says 41.0. The paper does not explain the difference.

activities.prompt: Ablations from Table 3. Each row changes one part of the base model, retrains it and scores it on a separate set of practice sentences used for testing choices, not the final test. The unchanged base model scores 25.8 BLEU there.

cases.label: One attention head instead of eight
cases.text: 24.9 BLEU, 0.9 lower. A 'head' is one copy of the ask–score–blend attention step. The base model runs eight side by side, and each can look for something different. More is not always better: 32 heads gave 25.4.

cases.label: No dropout
cases.text: 24.6 BLEU, 1.2 lower. Dropout randomly switches off parts of the network during training so it cannot simply memorise its examples. Without it, the model over-fits.

cases.label: Learned positions instead of sine waves
cases.text: 25.7 BLEU, almost the same as 25.8. Letting the network learn its own position stamps works about as well. The authors kept sine waves because they may cope with sentences longer than any seen in training.

activities.takeaway: Ablations show which parts carry weight. Several heads and dropout matter. The exact kind of position stamp barely does. Each variant was trained once, on one language pair, with no error bars, so gaps of a few tenths of a point are hard to read.

activities.question: Which passage supports the claim that the Transformer reaches top translation quality with very little training time?

options.quote: The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.
options.feedback: Yes. This sentence links quality (a new state of the art) to time (twelve hours on eight GPUs). It also gives the reason: the work can be split up and run in parallel, because no step-by-step chain has to be waited on.

options.quote: In row (E) we replace our sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings [9], and observe nearly identical results to the base model.
options.feedback: This is an ablation result about position stamps. It shows that two versions score about the same, but it says nothing about training time.

options.quote: This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.
options.feedback: This is about a training trick called label smoothing and how it affects scores. It concerns quality, not speed, and it shows that different measures can disagree.

hints: Look for a sentence that mentions both quality and time.
One option gives a number of hours.

activities.question: The Transformer got the highest BLEU scores. Which reading of that fact do you find best supported?

options.text: Its translations are simply better, in every way a human reader would care about.
options.feedback: This goes beyond the evidence. BLEU counts wording overlap with reference translations. It does not check meaning, fluency or style directly, and the paper reports no human ratings. The paper itself shows that measures can disagree: label smoothing 'hurts perplexity' but 'improves accuracy and BLEU score'.

options.text: On these two news test sets, its wording matched human reference translations more closely than earlier systems did.
options.feedback: This is the reading closest to what was measured. Its limits: only two language pairs, both from English, and only news text. The parsing experiment hints that the design carries over to other tasks, but it is a single extra task, not a broad survey.

options.text: The gains come purely from the new architecture.
options.feedback: This is partly supported. The cost comparison and the ablations point to the design. But the final scores also used other choices: averaging the last few saved copies of the model, a tuned search for the best output sentence, and label smoothing. These were not removed one by one when comparing against rival systems.

options.text: A 2-point BLEU gap could be luck, so we can't tell anything.
options.feedback: The caution is fair: the paper gives no error bars, and each variant was trained once. But 'nothing' is too strong. The base model also beat every earlier entry, the big model beat ensembles by more than 2 points, and both did so at lower cost. Those results point the same way, though none settles the question alone.

activities.question: Put the whole lesson together. What did this paper show that changed how people build translation systems?

options.text: A network that drops step-by-step reading entirely, letting every word look at every other word in one step, translated better than all earlier systems while training in as little as 12 hours on one machine.
options.feedback: Yes, this is the core finding. Attention had been used before, but alongside recurrent networks. Removing the recurrent chain let all the work run in parallel. The base model beat every earlier entry after 12 hours on one 8-GPU machine, and the big model set new records.

options.text: Adding attention to recurrent networks made them faster to train.
options.feedback: Earlier systems already combined attention with recurrent networks. The paper's point is the opposite: drop the recurrence entirely and rely on attention alone.

options.text: It won mainly by being far bigger and training far longer than its rivals.
options.feedback: Table 2 says otherwise. The base model had the lowest training cost listed and still beat every earlier entry. Even the big model cost less than the leading ensembles.

options.text: It proved the Transformer is the best design for every language task.
options.feedback: The evidence is narrower: two translation benchmarks and one grammar (parsing) task, all graded with automatic scores. The authors list other kinds of data, such as images and audio, as future work.

hints: Recall concept 6: what did self-attention replace, and why did that speed up training?
Pick the option that combines better scores, lower cost and no step-by-step chain.

Adds a side-by-side view of aligned, perpendicular and opposite arrows before practice, to anchor the three cases.

A worked numeric example walks through the three steps one at a time. A match task then pairs query, key and value with their everyday roles (a search request, a label on a folder, the folder's contents).

options.why: The learner raises the list length with scaling off and watches the learning signal collapse, then turns scaling on to rescue it. The check asks for a setting where scaling matters.
Staged steps follow the paper's chain of reasoning (bigger dimension, then bigger scores, then saturated softmax, then tiny gradients) before the learner practises on the curves.

plan.why: First a side-by-side comparison shows two reordered sentences getting identical attention blends. Then the learner slides the position and finds two positions whose stamps differ clearly.

options.why: First a side-by-side comparison shows two reordered sentences getting identical attention blends. Then the learner slides the position and finds two positions whose stamps differ clearly.
After practice, a choice question asks why the authors kept fixed sine waves when learned stamps worked about as well (they hoped the waves would extend to longer sentences).

plan.why: The learner lengthens the sentence and compares step counts. They then find the sentence length where attention's total work exceeds a recurrent layer's, which shows the trade-off the paper states.

options.why: The learner lengthens the sentence and compares step counts. They then find the sentence length where attention's total work exceeds a recurrent layer's, which shows the trade-off the paper states.
